lesson.title: Maximum demand: what the whole building draws

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the neutral bar fall from 24.35 A to 0.30 A, as the phase bars even out, when you move DBL2’s circuits off L1 and share them across all three phases.
interactive.title: What the whole building draws
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A refresher lesson in twelve screens on maximum demand: what the whole building draws, how it is shared across the three phases, and diversity. Back and Continue move between the screens. Screen 1, Do you still have it?: "There is a diversity percentage for lighting circuits. Is diversity a rule you must apply?" Three choices, in this order: "Yes: BS 7671 sets the percentages"; "No: it is guidance, used where common sense allows"; "Yes, wherever the On-Site Guide gives a percentage". Right: "Still there." The percentages come only from the On-Site Guide, so they are guidance and need not be applied.[^1] Ten 100 W lamps could be designed at 660 W rather than 1000 W.[^2] Then the two slips, a line each, and two buttons: Refresh the why (on to screen 2) and Skip to the practice (straight to screen 7). Wrong, the first: BS 7671 has no diversity table. Under Regulation 311.1 the designer assesses maximum demand and may take diversity into account, and the On-Site Guide gives the recognised figures.[^3] Wrong, the third: even where it gives one, you may leave it off. 66% for a domestic lighting circuit[^4] and 90% for a shop's lighting[^5] are On-Site Guide figures, used only where the loads really do not all run together.[^1] Then the right answer, and on to screen 2 with no skip. Read: diversity is guidance, not a rule. Screen 2, What it is for: maximum demand is the largest current an installation draws at any one time.[^6] You size the supply and each submain from it. Regulation 311.1 lets you work it out for the whole installation or for one part,[^7] so each board gets its own figure. Question 10 of the assignment asks for it. You may make informed assumptions where you need to.[^8] It links to question 1b, on balancing the loads.[^9][^10] In red, if it is skipped or wrong: too low, and the supply fuse or a submain's device and cable carries more than it was chosen for. Too high, and the cables are bigger and dearer than they need be.[^11] One line: a figure with diversity is an estimate, and it may occasionally be exceeded.[^12] Screen 3, The why: each of DBL2's lighting circuits runs between one line and the neutral. Equal currents on L1, L2 and L3 cancel in the neutral,[^13] but unequal ones do not.[^14] So the neutral carries the imbalance, and the heaviest phase sets what the supply must carry.[^15] The picture: three columns, L1, L2 and L3, each holding the circuit cards on it, and four bars on one scale that fits 24.35 A: L1, L2, L3 and N, each with its current. Seven cards, one for each of DBL2's circuits (screen 8 gives what each feeds), each with a short name and its current: C1 Consultation 4.89 A; C2 Toilets W 4.08 A; C3 Toilets E and tea 5.71 A; C4 Stores 2.63 A; C5 Showroom E 3.33 A; C6 Reception 2.50 A; C7 Foyer 1.21 A. It opens with all seven on L1: L1 24.35 A, N 24.35 A. "Drag a card to another phase, or tap it to move it on." Two buttons: All on L1, and Share them out (L1: C1 and C5, 8.22 A; L2: C3 and C6, 8.21 A; L3: C2, C4 and C7, 7.92 A; N 0.30 A). Two readouts: Heaviest phase, whose label names the phase, and Neutral. Under them the rule for currents at about the same power factor: IN = √(I1² + I2² + I3² − I1·I2 − I2·I3 − I3·I1). It adds three currents that are a third of a cycle apart. It holds for mains-frequency currents only: fluorescent and LED fittings also draw third-harmonic currents, which add in the neutral instead of cancelling. Lesson 4 covers those. One line: the card currents use practice values from screen 6. Read: put all seven on L1, and the neutral carries 24.35 A, as much as L1. Share them out, and it carries just 0.30 A, harmonics aside. The heaviest phase is then 8.22 A. Screen 4, Check: "A board's lighting circuits carry 10 A on L1, 10 A on L2 and 4 A on L3, at about the same power factor. What does the neutral carry?" Choices: 24.00 A (added as if in step, but they are a third of a cycle apart, so they partly cancel), 6.00 A (right) and 0.00 A (only equal currents cancel completely). A Why? button: the 4 A on each phase cancels, leaving 6 A on L1 and 6 A on L2, which add to 6 A. By the rule, √(100 + 100 + 16 − 100 − 40 − 40) = √36 = 6.00 A. Read: the neutral carries 6.00 A. Screen 5, Diversity, as common sense: not every load runs flat out at once, so a building draws less than its connected load. Diversity means designing with common sense rather than for the maximum.[^16] The allowances used here are the On-Site Guide's for small shops, stores, offices and business premises. We treat the showroom as one of those. Commercial work may need measured loads instead.[^17] Lighting: 90% of the total current demand.[^5] Heating and power: 100% of the largest appliance plus 75% of the rest.[^18] Motors: 100% of the largest, 80% of the second largest and 60% of the rest; the showroom has only one.[^19] Standard circuits: 100% of the largest circuit plus 50% of every other.[^20] Only these four are used here; the rest are in Appendix A. EV charge points: no diversity, a factor of 1, unless a load management system controls them.[^21] Regulation 722.311 lets load curtailment count,[^22] and on this job load management is optional.[^23] In a fold, Where it's argued: some say BS 7671 does not forbid diversity on EV points,[^24] and others that without load management you still allow none.[^25] Some apply 66% to a single lighting circuit's Ib.[^2] Others apply diversity only to the total at the origin.[^26] Another view is that it is only rarely right for one circuit.[^27] Another method applies a factor to the loads on each board.[^28] Where they are mainly lighting, it advises a factor close to 1.[^29] Then what we assume: all the lighting at 100%, because question 5a has the internal showroom lights on from 7.30 am to 9 pm, and we take the rest of the lighting with them. The On-Site Guide would allow 90%: a designer's call. Screen 6, Worked example, a line at each press. Ten 100 W lamps: 10 × 100 = 1000 W; 1000 × 0.66 = 660 W.[^2] Ib 660 ÷ 230 = 2.87 A against 1000 ÷ 230 = 4.35 A, so a smaller cable.[^11] Then one 4 × 36 W modular fitting from the drawing's key:[^30] 4 × 36 = 144 W of tubes. Tube watts leave out the ballast,[^31] and 25% may be allowed when no loss is given,[^32] so 144 × 1.25 = 180 W. At 0.96, an electronic ballast's power factor,[^33] 180 ÷ (230 × 0.96) = 180 ÷ 220.8 = 0.82 A. One 26 W LED fitting:[^34] at 0.95, one maker's power factor for a similar panel[^35] (another gives 0.97[^36]), 26 ÷ (230 × 0.95) = 26 ÷ 218.5 = 0.12 A. Marked as practice values: 25%, 0.96 and 0.95, since the drawing does not name the fittings' gear. On a real job, use the maker's figures; a separate driver's watts are extra.[^37] One line: an older method takes lamp watts × 1.8 ÷ voltage for discharge lighting, at a power factor of at least 0.85.[^38][^39] We use the first method. Screen 7, Section A, question 3 (a): the showroom's scenario panel,[^40][^41] and how we split the building. DBL2 sits in the tools and warranty store and feeds the east of the building: the consultation bay, the toilets, cleaner and tea bay, the two stores, the showroom east of the welcome desk, service reception, the foyer and the walkway bollards. DBL1 feeds the rest. Counted on the lighting drawing, DBL2's share is 55 LED 26 W, 18 modular 4 × 36 W, 4 twin 58 W and 6 walkway bollards 18 W.[^34][^30][^42][^43] The key does not say whether a twin's 58 W is each tube or the whole fitting. We take two 58 W tubes, 116 W, the cautious reading. "(a) Determine the connected lighting load of DBL2, from the key's wattages." A typed answer (part 3a, in W, whole watts): 55 × 26 = 1430 W; 18 × 144 = 2592 W; 4 × 116 = 464 W; 6 × 18 = 108 W; 4594 W. Slips: 2650 W (each modular fitting as 36 W, but it holds four tubes), 4486 W (the bollards left out), 4362 W (each twin as 58 W in all, the other reading of the key). Read: DBL2's connected lighting load is 4594 W. Screen 8, Section A, question 3 (b): (a) carried forward at 4594 W. DBL2's seven circuits, as we split them, with what each feeds and its watts: C1 consultation bay, 6 modular, 864 W; C2 uni-sex and female toilets, 5 modular, 720 W; C3 cleaner, male toilets and tea bay, 7 modular, 1008 W; C4 the two stores, 4 twin, 464 W; C5 showroom east, 28 LED, 728 W; C6 service reception, 21 LED, 546 W; C7 foyer, 6 LED and 6 bollards, 264 W. The phases: L1 C1 and C5; L2 C3 and C6; L3 C2, C4 and C7. The rules from screen 6, with their practice values. "(b) Determine the current on L1." A typed answer (part 3b): C1, 864 × 1.25 = 1080 W, 1080 ÷ 220.8 = 4.89 A; C5, 728 ÷ 218.5 = 3.33 A; 4.89 + 3.33 = 8.22 A. Slips: 7.24 A (the ballast left out), 7.87 A (the power factor left out), 10.09 A (the older × 1.8 method, where this question uses the 25% allowance), 24.35 A (the whole board, where L1 carries only its own circuits). After it: L2, 5.71 + 2.50 = 8.21 A; L3, 4.08 + 2.63 + 1.21 = 7.92 A; the neutral 0.30 A. Lesson 8 sizes DBL2's submain on the heaviest phase, 8.22 A. After two misses the working is shown, and part (c) carries on from 8.22 A. Read: L1 carries 8.22 A. Screen 9, Section A, question 3 (c): 1(a) and 3(b) carried forward (23.08 A, 8.22 A). Given, each practice value marked. Lighting at 100%, as question 5a has the showroom lights on from 7.30 am to 9 pm: DBL2 8.22 + 8.21 + 7.92 = 24.35 A, and DBL1 38.74 A. DBL1 is worked the same way from its 103 LED, 16 modular, 12 twin and 6 bulkheads, with the bulkheads taken with the LEDs and no ballast allowance. Its 9 wall spots (2 × 35 W)[^44] and 6 columns (70 W)[^45] are taken at a power factor of 0.9, a practice value with no source, as the lamps are not named. Sockets: eight 32 A circuits, one per area, each taken at its rating, as standard circuits: 100% of the largest plus 50% of every other. Fixed points: three 20 A DP switches[^46] and a 32 A rotary isolator,[^47] each taken at its rating, as heating and power: 100% of the largest plus 75% of the rest. EV: two charging points, each with two 32 A outlets,[^48][^49] taken as four single-phase outlets with no diversity. That is a practice value, as the drawing does not say whether the outlets are single- or three-phase. The 63 A TPN isolators are not part of the circuit. The motor at 100%, as the only one.[^19] The single-phase loads shared evenly, so their total is divided by 3.[^50] "(c) Determine the maximum demand of the installation, per phase." A typed answer (part 3c): 63.09 + 144.00 + 77.00 + 128.00 = 412.09 A; 412.09 ÷ 3 = 137.36 A; 137.36 + 23.08 = 160.44 A. Unrounded working gives 160.44 A too, and the last place either side is accepted. Slips: 202.78 A (no diversity), 137.36 A (the motor left out), 145.05 A (the motor divided by 3, though its Ib is already a line current), 435.17 A (not shared over three phases), 158.34 A (the lighting at 90%, fair for a designer, but the question takes 100%). After it: about 160 A a phase, an estimate on practice values, which question 10 allows. A real split is heavier on one phase. Four 32 A EV outlets cannot share evenly over three phases, so one phase carries two: 2 × 32 = 64 A, against an even share of 128 ÷ 3 = 42.67 A. That phase stays heavier unless other circuits move off it. Read: about 160.44 A a phase. Screen 10, Section B: "State two reasons a designer applies diversity." Dan writes an answer, marked against four points; any two make a full answer. He gets one more go, then the model answer. Screen 11, Section A, changed numbers: "A small office has a single-phase board. It feeds five 32 A socket circuits, arranged as standard circuits, and lighting with a total current demand of 18.00 A. Use the allowances for small shops, stores and offices: standard circuits at 100% of the largest plus 50% of every other, and lighting at 90%. Determine its maximum demand." A typed answer: 32 + 0.5 × 4 × 32 = 96.00 A; 0.9 × 18.00 = 16.20 A; 112.20 A. Slips: 178.00 A (no diversity), 114.00 A (the lighting at 100%), 96.20 A (50% on the largest circuit too). Read: 112.20 A. Screen 12, Keep this: the summary card, then Finish the lesson. The caption under the lesson says practice values are marked and each line is worked from the rounded figure before it. It shows only on screens 3, 4, 6 to 9 and 11.
interactive.ignores: The bars treat each circuit's current as in step with its own line voltage, as if every fitting had the same power factor; theirs differ a little (0.95 and 0.96 here), which changes the neutral current very little. The circuit currents rest on practice values for ballast loss and power factor, not on the makers' data for the drawing's own fittings. Harmonics are left out: fluorescent and LED fittings can draw third-harmonic currents, which add in the neutral instead of cancelling; that is lesson 4. The bars show steady currents with every fitting on, not switching on, dimming or a lamp failing.

explain.text:
[[Maximum demand]] is the largest current an installation draws at any one time.[^6] You can work it out for the whole installation or for one part of it.[^7] It is the current that the circuits, switches and protective devices feeding that part normally carry.[^51] So you choose the supply and each submain for it.

It is usually less than the connected load, because not everything runs flat out together. Allowing for that with common sense, rather than designing for the maximum, is [[diversity]].[^16] Its figures come from the On-Site Guide, and they are guidance, not a rule.[^1] A three-phase board raises a second question: which phase each single-phase circuit goes on.

Each lighting circuit runs between one line and the neutral, so its current comes back along the neutral. The three line voltages are a third of a cycle apart. Each circuit's current keeps step with its own line voltage, so the three currents are a third of a cycle apart too. Three equal currents spaced like that add up to nothing in the neutral. A balanced three-phase load has no neutral current at all.[^13] Make the currents unequal and they no longer cancel.[^14] What is left over flows in the neutral. So the neutral carries the imbalance, not the total.

Take DBL2's seven lighting circuits, using practice values for the fittings. Put them all on L1, and L1 and the neutral both carry 24.35 A. Share them out, and the phases carry 8.22, 8.21 and 7.92 A. The neutral then carries just 0.30 A. That is why you spread single-phase circuits about equally across the three phases.[^52] It is also why the heaviest phase, not the average, sets what the supply must carry.[^15]

This picture is simplified. It treats every fitting as having the same power factor and drawing a smooth current. Real power factors differ a little, which hardly moves the neutral current. But fluorescent and LED fittings can also draw third-harmonic currents. Those add in the neutral instead of cancelling. Lesson 4 covers them.

Diversity takes the total down by type of load. For small shops, stores and offices, the On-Site Guide allows 100% of the largest standard circuit and 50% of every other.[^20] BS 7671 itself has no such table and leaves the assessment to the designer.[^3]

Where to apply diversity is argued. Some apply 66% to a single lighting circuit's Ib.[^2] Others apply it only to the total at the origin.[^26] Another view is that it is only rarely right for a single circuit's design current.[^27] For EV charge points without load management, allow no diversity: a factor of 1.[^21] We follow that here, though it is argued.

Common sense can also say no diversity at all. Question 5a has the internal showroom lights on from 7.30 am to 9 pm. So we take all the lighting at 100%. That is a designer's call.

**Maximum demand is the connected load, with diversity only where common sense allows.**[^53] **Share it across L1, L2 and L3 so the heaviest phase is as light as it can be.**[^52]

analogy.text: Think of a dockyard canteen. The cooks plan for the busiest sitting, not for everyone on the base eating at once: that is diversity. And they split the diners evenly between three serving counters, decided in advance, so that no one queue sets the pace for the whole room: that is sharing the circuits across L1, L2 and L3.
analogy.breaks: Hungry people can wait. Current cannot. If everything does come on together, the installation carries it there and then. That is why a figure with diversity may occasionally be exceeded.[^12] It is also why EV points without load management get no diversity.[^21] And three uneven queues just leave one long one. Uneven phase currents also send the difference down the neutral.

practice.text:
- List every load on a schedule of circuits:[^54] each board's circuits, what they feed and their current.
- Work each load's current from what it really draws. For lighting, use the key's watts with the ballast loss and power factor from the maker's data.[^31] Until you have that data, use practice values.[^32] Work a motor's Ib as in lesson 1.
- Share the single-phase circuits about equally across L1, L2 and L3,[^52] and add up each phase. The heaviest phase sets the size.[^15]
- Apply diversity by type of load where common sense allows, from Appendix A of the On-Site Guide. Write down why. Leave it off where the loads run together, such as the showroom's lighting. Leave it off EV points without load management too.[^21]
- Add each three-phase load's line current to every phase. Then compare the heaviest phase with the supply.
- Check each board against the device that feeds it. The board's rating must be at least that device's, or its full connected load must fit. Diversity sizes the supply and submains, never the board.

**Rule of thumb:** when you cannot tell whether loads run together, take them at 100%. Too high a figure costs money. Too low a figure leaves the supply and submains carrying more than they were chosen for.

**Worked example:** the showroom, question 10, using the practice values. Lighting: 24.35 + 38.74 = 63.09 A. Eight 32 A socket circuits as standard circuits: 32 + 0.5 × 7 × 32 = 144.00 A.[^20] The 32 A point and three 20 A points as heating and power: 32 + 0.75 × 3 × 20 = 77.00 A.[^18] Four 32 A EV outlets: 128.00 A. Together that is 412.09 A, or 137.36 A a phase when shared evenly. Add the motor's 23.08 A on every line, and you get 160.44 A a phase.

**Common mistakes**
- Treating diversity as a rule. It is guidance and need not be applied.[^1]
- Putting every single-phase circuit on one phase. The neutral then carries the lot.
- Using fluorescent tube watts alone. The ballast's loss is extra.[^31]
- Dividing the motor's current by three with the rest. A three-phase load's Ib is already a line current.
- Applying diversity to EV charge points without load management. We take none, though it is argued.[^25]

b1.q: State two reasons a designer applies diversity.

points.text: Not every load runs at full current at the same time, so the real demand is less than the connected load. Diversity means designing with common sense rather than for the maximum.

You can choose the supply and submains for the demand they will really carry, not for every load at once. A board is different. Its rating must cover the device that feeds it, or its whole connected load taken at 100%. Otherwise load management must cap its demand.
points.cite: Slides p.10 (design using 'common sense' rather than the maximum demand); BS 7671:2018+A4:2026 Regulation 536.4.202 (SELECT A4 overview, in research)

b1.model: Not every load runs at full current at the same time. So designing for every load at once overstates what the installation draws. Diversity means designing with common sense rather than for the maximum. It keeps cable sizes smaller and costs lower. It also lets you choose the supply and submains for the demand they will really carry. A board's own rating is not cut by diversity. It must cover the device that feeds it, or its whole connected load, unless load management caps the demand. The figures come from the On-Site Guide. They are guidance, used with judgement, not a rule.

summary.title: Maximum demand and diversity
summary.for: The largest current the installation, or one board, draws at any one time. You size the supply and every submain from it. Under Regulation 311.1 the designer assesses it.
summary.rule:
Lighting: I = W ÷ (230 × pf), fluorescent tube W × 1.25 first if no ballast loss is given
Neutral, same pf, no harmonics: IN = √(I1² + I2² + I3² − I1·I2 − I2·I3 − I3·I1)
Per phase, shared evenly: single-phase total after diversity ÷ 3, + each three-phase line current

Share single-phase circuits about equally over L1, L2 and L3. The heaviest phase sets the size.
Diversity figures are guidance, not a rule. Use them only where common sense allows.
A board is never sized by diversity. The device feeding it is no bigger than its rating, or its full connected load fits, or load management caps it.
EV points without load management: take no diversity. Some argue otherwise.

traps.text: Diversity treated as a rule. It is guidance and need not be applied. Nor does it ever keep a board, or an RCCB in it, from overload.

checks.label: The rule gives the case file's seven circuit currents: 4.89, 4.08, 5.71, 2.63, 3.33, 2.50 and 1.21 A
All seven on L1: L1 and the neutral both carry 24.35 A, the whole board
Shared out: 8.22, 8.21 and 7.92 A on the phases, 0.30 A in the neutral
Three equal currents leave nothing in the neutral; one phase alone sends it all back
Whatever the arrangement, the neutral never carries more than the heaviest phase
Sharing out from all on L1 takes five moves, one card at a time, and ends on the split
The check: 10, 10 and 4 A leave 6.00 A in the neutral; added, 24.00 A
The worked example: 660 W, 2.87 A against 4.35 A; 180 W and 0.82 A for a modular fitting; 0.12 A for an LED
Every slip lies outside its answer's accepted range
Lighting in a shop: 90% of the total current demand
Standard circuits: 100% of the largest circuit + 50% of every other
Heating and power: 100% of the largest appliance + 75% of the remaining
If no power-loss value is given for the ballast, 25% of the tube watts may be used
cos φ = 0.96 for an electronic ballast

applied.problem: Three overstatements: maximum demand is not always less than the connected load (the lesson itself takes the lighting and EV points at 100%); the 0.30 A neutral ignores the third harmonics that slides p.33 say fluorescent banks draw; and question 5a covers only the internal showroom lights, not all…

The card states 'None on EV points without load management' as a rule, though since Amendment 1 BS 7671 lets load curtailment count and the forum argues it; the neutral formula and the ÷ 3 line hold only without harmonics and for an even share.
Called a trap outright, but whether EV points may take diversity without load management is argued (gkenyon: BS 7671 does not prohibit it); the card should say it is the course's choice.

The last common mistake states as settled that EV points take no diversity without load management; the lesson's own sources argue it ([^24] against [^25]), so it should say this is the course's choice.
'why EV points without load management get none' states a contested point as fact; it is the course's choice (the IEC wording), argued on the IET forum.

Screen 5 says question 5a has 'the showroom lights on together', but 5a (pack p.4) covers only the internal showroom lights; the course takes all the lighting, toilets, stores and outside lights too, at 100% as its own call.

notes.problem: The trap's cite leads with 'BS 7671 722.311.201 (NAPIT)', but that regulation (Amendment 1) lets load curtailment count and does not itself forbid diversity on EV points; the no-diversity wording is the IEC text in the Schneider guide. Cites are frozen here: worth re-pointing at review.

C7's walkway bollards (and DBL1's 18 W bulkheads) are worked at the LED power factor 0.95, while the wall spots and columns, equally unnamed, take 0.9; the screens never say which practice value the bollards use. The figures are right as worked (264 ÷ 218.5 = 1.21 A); worth one word on screen 8.
